Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Vignette:
For twenty-nine years, Leo Tran had stood in courtrooms and argued for the accused. He had been a public defender long enough to believe that even the worst moments in a person’s life could be shaped into a coherent story, presented to a jury, and resolved. That belief ended on a Tuesday evening in November, two years ago, when his wife, Mai, collapsed in their kitchen while washing rice. Leo heard the thud from the living room and found her on the tile floor, her face turned away from him. He called 911, he remembered that, but what he remembered next came only in fragments—the sound of the paramedic’s radio crackling a series of numbers he could not make sense of, the sight of Mai’s slipper lying on its side near the stove, the way his own voice sounded far away when he tried to answer their questions. He could not put those pieces together in order no matter how many times he tried. When he closed his eyes, he heard the radio again, that staticky burst of syllables that meant nothing to him but that he was certain, in the moment, meant something terrible was about to happen.

In the months that followed, Leo did not tell anyone that his memories came in broken pieces. He told his colleagues that he was fine, that he was taking some time, that he would be back soon. He did go back, eventually, but the first day he walked into the courthouse, he found himself scanning every face in the hallway with a speed that felt automatic and exhausting. He was looking for someone dangerous, though he could not have said who. What he noticed instead was how many people there were, how close they stood, how easily a person could be hidden in a crowd. He began arriving an hour early so he could enter the building before the rush, and he left as soon as his last case was called, walking to his car with his keys already between his fingers. At home, the checking started quietly—he would touch the front door lock before bed, then check it again before he turned off the light, then get up once more to be absolutely certain. He knew it was locked. He had checked it three times. He checked it again anyway.

Leo had always been a man who ate methodically, but after Mai died, he found himself standing in front of the refrigerator at ten o’clock at night, eating leftover noodles straight from the container without tasting them. It was not hunger. It was a way to stop his mind from replaying the sound of the paramedic’s radio, a way to fill the silence in the apartment with something other than the fragmented images that rose up without warning. He gained weight, but he did not care. What he cared about was the television. He had always watched the evening news, but now he could not bear it. Any story about a sudden death, a heart attack, a person collapsing in their home—he would feel his chest tighten and his throat close, and he would turn it off mid-sentence. He stopped watching hospital dramas entirely. He cancelled his streaming subscriptions for crime documentaries. His daughter called him one evening and asked if he had seen a particular film that was nominated for awards, and he said no, he had not, and he did not explain why.

What frightened Leo most was the way his body reacted to nothing at all. He would be sitting in his office, reviewing a file, and suddenly his heart would pound as if someone had shouted in his ear. His hands would shake. He would look around the room and find nothing wrong—no threat, no danger, no reason for the terror that flooded through him. But the feeling was real. He had come to believe that his own body was lying to him, that it had become a faulty alarm that rang for no reason, and that there was no way to trust himself anymore. And underneath all of that, what he felt when he remembered Mai was not the fear. It was the grief. It came over him like a wave that knocked him sideways, and when he remembered her hands in the sink, the rice grains scattered on the counter, he would hear her voice in his head saying something ordinary—his name, maybe, or asking him what he wanted for dinner—and he would have to sit down because the loss was as fresh as the day it happened.

He came to therapy because his daughter told him she was worried. She said he was not himself. Leo did not know what that meant anymore. He was afraid that if he let himself feel the grief fully, he would not be able to function at all. But he was also tired of checking the locks.
